newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Dr John, always in the right place.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Dr John, always in the right place.

text.p: Dr John has a knack of being in the right place at the wrong time. Fortunately, it always seems to work out well for the master of the New Orleans piano.
Like the time he got shot.

If he had not tried to wrestle a gun away from a man in a bar, maybe Mac Rebennack would never have become Dr John or his alter-ego, the flamboyant "Night Tripper." Maybe rock, jazz and rhythm and blues would never have heard his rollicking piano style.
"I got shot through here and it came out here," he said matter-of-factly, holding up his left hand with the little finger bent almost at a right angle above the top joint.

"This guy was trying to kill the singer with our band," he continued in his gentle New Orleans lilt. "The singer was real young and his mother said if anything happened to him on the road she was going to take this butcher knife and chop my nuts off," he said with a laugh. "I was thinking about her somewhere in my mind as this guy was pistol-whipping him, I went to get the gun out of his hand and I got shot."

The injury was a turning point in then-guitar-player Rebennack's musical career. "I don't even remember to bring the guitar when we do gigs (now)," he told Reuters in an interview. "On this (latest) record I play one song on the guitar but because I got shot in the finger it aggravates me."

After a nearly 40-year career, Dr John has made his first completely live album, "Trippin' Live," recorded at legendary Ronnie Scott's club in London. A gumbo of his favourites from Mardi Gras Indian songs and New Orleans blues to his 1973 Top Ten hit as Dr John and the Medicine Show, "Right Place, Wrong Time," it allows him to celebrate his musical roots
FROM ROLLING STONES TO ERIC CLAPTON

Since his recording career began in 1968 with the album "Gris-Gris," Dr John has played with everyone from the Rolling Stones and Bob Dylan to Eric Clapton and Van Morrison. His versatility has allowed him to explore other musical forms, and in 1989 he won a Grammy for a duet with Rickie Lee Jones on an album of classics by Cole Porter and others.

He won a second Grammy for "Goin' Back to New Orleans," an album with such Crescent City friends as the Neville Brothers. And this year he won a third Grammy for a star-studded album tribute to blues guitarist Stevie Ray Vaughan.

As Rebennack sees it, living in New Orleans it is hard not to become imbued with a rich musical tradition. "That's what New Orleans is all about, someone just getting out there and having fun," said the 55-year-old singer whose physique bears testimony to the Southern city's equally-important tradition -- its cuisine.

His father, who he thinks was of French-Basque extraction, was a record salesman, so he grew up hearing all kinds of music. "Most of the records he sold were early be-bop and so-called race records, blues, rhythm and blues, gospel, traditional jazz and hillbilly records."

But in all that sound, Rebennack remembers when he knew he would be a musician. "I know what song it was, it was Joe Turner singing 'Piney Brown' (with) Pete Johnson on the piano. I told my father -- I was about 4-years-old -- 'I want to play the piano, I want to play like that guy, who is it?' and he said, 'Pete Johnson and don't forget it.'"
'WATCH THE PIANO PLAYER'

But the young Dr John-to-be actually began by taking guitar lessons. "My guitar teacher told me: 'Watch the piano player, to learn the chords.' I learned not only that but I learned how to play piano from watching.
"I got kicked out of school in the ninth grade and went on the road," said the musician, who is rarely seen without his trademark beret and silver-tipped walking stick.

"Then I was hanging with James Booker and real good piano players. I learned to play not only from watching them but from playing guitar with them. Alan Toussaint, Professor Longhair ... a lot of piano players taught me stuff. James Booker actually taught me how to play different guys' styles."
But it was not until that fateful bullet in the finger that Rebennack began to take the piano seriously and in 1961 he was hired to play several shows on the organ.

"I was playing behind strippers and exotic dancers and comedians, then four hours at another club, four hours at a jam session. I was working from midnight to noon. I was so burned out, but it was my first keyboard gig," he said.

It is the piano that reflects his soul. "It's always been something I wrote on. It's a fundamental instrument for music. It's like a whole orchestra rolled into one and nothing feels like a piano," he said.

A natural story-teller, he summed up what music means to him and to many in New Orleans: "I was still taking guitar lessons when my father passed (died) and I was bummed out and my guitar teacher said 'Why don't you go to your daddy's grave and play him some songs?'
"So I did that and sat down in the cemetery and I was sitting on his grave playing the guitar and I felt better. He (the teacher) told me he did that with his daddy."
